title: To Save Democracy, Look to the Arctic Woolly Bear Moth
gist: Jonathon Keats argues there is no optimal level of constitutional entrenchment — governments fail both when constitutions calcify and when they are too easily rewritten — and proposes borrowing insect holometaboly: constitutions with staged life phases, clauses carrying built-in deactivation, and environmental triggers, using data showing only 50% of national constitutions outlast Jefferson's 19-year generation and that modern constitutions are amended twice a decade at four times the length of the 1789 US document.

insights.claim: Governments fail both because constitutions are too strong and because they are too weak, so there is no optimal level of entrenchment and no fine-tuning of flexibility and specificity that solves democratic governance.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Reframes institutional-stability risk: reform proposals that only adjust amendment difficulty are structurally incapable of fixing governance fragility.
insights.quote: There appears to be no optimal level of entrenchment, no fine-tuning of flexibility and specificity to solve the problem of democratic governance.
insights.locator: The truth is that governments fail because constitutions are too strong

insights.claim: Legal scholars Sanford Levinson and Jack Balkin define two types of constitutional crisis: type one, where political leaders publicly claim the right to suspend features of the constitution to preserve social order, and type two, where all actors comply with their constitutional duties but following the accepted understanding fails to resolve the crisis or leads to disaster.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: A usable taxonomy for pricing political risk: type-two crises are the common, slow-burn variety that erode legitimacy without any visible rule-breaking.
insights.quote: when all relevant actors comply with their widely accepted constitutional duties and roles, but following the accepted understandings of the Constitution fails to resolve an existing political crisis or leads to disaster

insights.claim: Eight out of ten Americans across the political spectrum consider democracy to be at risk, reflecting a legitimacy crisis produced by the combination of constitutional constraints on majoritarianism.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Cross-partisan legitimacy erosion is a structural, not cyclical, US political-risk input.
insights.locator: Even more threatening is the crisis of legitimacy

insights.claim: The mechanisms by which US political minorities obtain disproportionate influence — Senate apportionment, the electoral college and lifetime appointment of federal judges — are all written into the Constitution rather than being distortions of it.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Because the grievance is constitutional by design, it cannot be litigated away — only amended, which the same document makes nearly impossible.

insights.claim: Only 27 amendments have passed since 1789, considerably less than 1% of the number advanced, making the US amendment process unwieldy even though it is easier than changing the Articles of Confederation.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Quantifies the near-zero base rate of formal US constitutional change — expect adaptation to happen through interpretation and executive action instead.
insights.locator: Amendment is considerably easier than changes

themes.theme: The US founding as constitutional crisis

insights.claim: The Articles of Confederation failed operationally because Congress had to requisition soldiers and money from sovereign states that routinely sent less than requested, imperiling credit, credibility and national security.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Classic case study in how a federation without direct taxing and conscription power becomes fiscally and militarily non-viable.
insights.locator: Almost immediately, the Articles proved dysfunctional

insights.claim: The US Constitution came into being through a constitutional crisis: conventioneers ignored the Articles' unanimity requirement and transformed the Virginia Plan into a compact needing only nine states' consent, leaving holdouts little choice but to accept.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The founding precedent is that fundamental institutional change happened by rule-breaking, not by process — a template that recurs in constitutional stress episodes.
insights.quote: The founding irony of the United States Constitution is that it came into being by way of a constitutional crisis.

insights.claim: Virginia governor Edmund Randolph justified exceeding the convention's mandate in June 1787 with the argument that there are great seasons when persons with limited powers are justified in exceeding them.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The emergency-exception rhetoric that legitimated the US founding is the same rhetoric used in modern claims to suspend constitutional constraints.

insights.claim: Athens' graphē paranomōn let any Assembly member halt voting and force a public jury trial on whether proposed legislation was contrary to legal custom, functioning as a nearly 200-year-old unwritten constitution limiting populist whim.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: An example of constitutional constraint enforced by procedure and juries rather than by a written document — a design option beyond entrenchment.
insights.locator: Every decision was made by simple majority

insights.claim: In 411 BCE the Athenian Assembly abolished the graphē paranomōn after oligarchs were blocked by it, and per John David Lewis this coincided with sophism's rise and rash decisions that allowed Sparta to defeat Athens in the Peloponnesian War.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Removing a constraint to defeat a faction destroyed the constraint's protective function for everyone — a recurring failure mode in institutional erosion.

insights.claim: The absence of a written constitution in Athens produced a type-two constitutional crisis in which the political system became self-defeating, showing that both excess constraint and excess freedom generate the same class of failure.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The failure mode is symmetrical, which is why the author rejects tuning flexibility as a solution.
insights.locator: In an irony as rich as any in Philadelphia

themes.theme: Modern constitutions drift Jeffersonian without gain

insights.claim: Mila Versteeg and Emily Zackin document that modern constitutions are typically amended twice per decade and are about four times the length of the document drafted in Philadelphia.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Global institutional design has already moved toward flexibility and specificity — the experiment has been run at scale.
insights.locator: As the legal scholars Mila Versteeg and Emily Zackin have documented

insights.claim: Rising constitutional specificity is a response to courts exploiting vagueness for political gain, while rising flexibility is a reaction against past generations ruling from beyond the grave — and both push constitutional law closer to ordinary legal code.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The drift trades away constitutional protection of longstanding norms for short-run alignment — a hidden cost in modern institutional design.
insights.locator: According to Versteeg and Zackin, increases in flexibility

insights.claim: Only 50% of national constitutions last longer than 19 years — the period Jefferson calculated as a generation — and although constitutions are becoming increasingly Jeffersonian there is scant evidence that democracy is stronger or more stable.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Hard evidence against the reformist assumption that easier constitutional change produces more durable democracy.
insights.quote: Jefferson’s dream endures as a recurring national nightmare

insights.claim: Jefferson advocated that the Constitution be rewritten by each generation, which he calculated as 19 years, but Madison prevailed — possibly aided by Jefferson being in Paris as minister to France during the Constitutional Convention.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Contingency, not deliberation, settled the founding design question — institutional outcomes hinge on who is in the room.
insights.locator: Thomas Jefferson argued that citizens needed to be deeply engaged

insights.claim: Jefferson's 1816 letter to Samuel Kercheval compared expecting a constitution to persist as written to requiring a man to wear the coat that fitted him as a boy, which the author reads as implying staged growth rather than periodic wholesale replacement.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Reinterprets the canonical argument for constitutional change as an argument for developmental staging — the essay's pivot.
insights.quote: wear still the coat which fitted him when a boy
insights.locator: Jefferson continued to contemplate these matters

insights.claim: The arctic woolly bear caterpillar Gynaephora groenlandica survives winter temperatures as low as -94 degrees Fahrenheit and summers reaching 60, feeding for only several weeks each June and entering freeze-tolerant diapause by early August before parasitoid wasps and flies become active, with a seven-year lifecycle extending to 14 years if food is scarce.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The empirical existence proof that staged development, not fine-tuned rigidity, is what survives extreme environmental variance.
insights.locator: As a result, the life of an Arctic woolly bear caterpillar

insights.claim: The woolly bear molts only when both conditions are met — enough willow consumed and the right time of year — so its life stages are simultaneously systematic and contingent, biologically entrenched without the peril of environmental misalignment.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The central design principle the author extracts: entrench the transition rules rather than the content, which dissolves the rigidity-versus-fragility tradeoff.
insights.quote: a tradeoff between entrenchment and flexibility is minimized by entrenching flex
insights.locator: But the dual regulation of molting based on time of year

insights.claim: Complete metamorphosis has been a successful survival strategy for at least 320 million years and through at least three mass extinctions, is used by more than 80% of extant insect species representing some 60% of Earth's animal life, and evolved only once on Earth.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Establishes staged development as one of the highest-performing organizational strategies in the historical record — an argument by revealed durability.
insights.locator: Holometaboly (the technical term for complete metamorphosis)

insights.claim: Holometaboly decouples the evolution of life stages into modules so growth and reproduction can each optimize semi-independently — efficient wings can become light and fragile precisely because they never have to withstand molting — which increases evolvability.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Modularity as the mechanism that converts staged design into faster adaptation — directly transferable to organizational and institutional architecture.
insights.locator: But an even more remarkable aspect of this life strategy is evolutionary

insights.claim: Total decoupling of life stages would be catastrophic, producing a temporal chimera biologically incompatible with itself, which is why much of the insect body remains intact through the pupa with adult structures like wing pads present but expressed at a whisper.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Staged systems need a persistent connective substrate — pure modularity without continuity destroys the organization.
insights.locator: Yet total decoupling would be catastrophic

insights.claim: Counterintuitively the adult insect form evolved first and the larval stage was added later — the larva is essentially an embryo on the move — because natural selection cannot make predictions and wing pads could not have evolved in advance of wings having any function.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Corrects the intuitive developmental narrative and shows that the flexible early stage is an added capability, not a primitive residue.

insights.claim: Some insects display polyphenism, a plurality of developmental pathways controlled by stimuli ranging from temperature to population size, so identical genomes yield adults with different physical and behavioural characteristics suited to their surroundings.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The biological basis for conditional, environment-triggered branching in institutional or organizational design.
insights.locator: In some insects (though not woolly bears), there's even a plurality

insights.claim: Sociologist William Starbuck's 1960s and 70s papers on organizational metamorphosis treated Karl Marx's historical materialism as the most famous metamorphosis model, in which new technologies such as farming and banking topple the ruling class when they become irreconcilable with older social structures — metamorphosis as disruption imposed from outside, not self-actuated transformation.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Frames technological disruption as involuntary regime change — the baseline against which self-directed corporate transformation is defined.

insights.claim: A popular midcentury model promulgated in the 1959 textbook Industrial Man held that businesses succeed by passing from founders to consolidators to administrators, undergoing internal rationalization followed by strategic optimization for external competition.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: A stage model of corporate maturity whose generality appealed to investors who could compound earnings by managing management.
insights.locator: According to one popular midcentury model

insights.claim: More recent management models seek to futureproof companies by making them agents of change that initiate the technological developments that would otherwise obsolete them, requiring periodic re-evaluation of corporate purpose lest the company persist in solving problems that no longer exist, plus radical alteration of the underlying business structure.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
entities: International Journal of Entrepreneurial Behaviour & Research
insights.so_what: A screen for durable compounders: does the firm re-derive its purpose and restructure, or is it optimizing a problem that has already disappeared?

insights.claim: The author's critique is that management literature invoking metamorphosis contains a complete and total absence of biology, using it as a cursory metaphor rather than a model — it could be replaced by generic terms like organizational transformation or paradigm shift with no loss.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The claim that the biological mechanism, not the metaphor, is the useful part — and it has never actually been applied.
insights.quote: In human affairs, metamorphosis has not been a model but rather a metaphor, and cursory even by metaphoric standards.

insights.claim: The fundamental transferable principle from insects is that resilience in a variable environment is managed by development in stages, where each stage is regulated differently and the regulation of those regulations accounts for the differences — insects have evolved multiple levels of regulation, governing everyday life and governing transition separately.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: The actionable design abstraction: separate operating rules from transition rules, a pattern applicable to any long-lived institution or organization.
insights.locator: The fundamental principle to be learned from bugs

insights.claim: The Articles of Confederation were structured for perpetuity rather than for metamorphosis, so replacement required suspending all the rules in Independence Hall when principles of perpetuity collided with harsh reality.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Designing for permanence guarantees that necessary change arrives as crisis — a general lesson for charters, treaties and corporate constitutions.

insights.claim: Constitutional clauses could be framed with future deactivation written into them, analogous to programmed cell death, with deactivated clauses reformulated according to higher-level rules — for example mandating state autonomy in a nation's early phase that is eliminated in a later one as assimilation increases.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: A concrete institutional-design primitive: sunset clauses with higher-order regeneration rules rather than plain expiry.
insights.locator: Like programmed cell death, where tissues self-destruct

insights.claim: A multiphase constitution would need external sensing, with relevant events from population change to climate extremes identified in advance and used as regulatory triggers, mirroring how the woolly bear gates development on internal condition and environment simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Trigger-based institutional change is testable and monitorable, unlike discretionary amendment.
insights.locator: A multiphase constitution must be sensitized in a similar manner

insights.claim: Existing precedents for staged constitutions include Brazil's 1988 constitution mandating a presidential system subject to a referendum five years later, Portugal's 1976 constitution forbidding amendments for six years to stabilize democracy after military dictatorship, and Aristotle's record of Athens enacting a constitution for the present crisis to be replaced by one drawn up for the future.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Transitional and expiring constitutions are an established practice, giving empirical precedent for the staged approach.

insights.claim: Constitutional scholar Sumit Bisarya likens transitional provisions to catalytic enzymes initiating a metabolic chain reaction, but the author argues they are better described as catalysts of constitutional embryogenesis, since they only set initial conditions rather than governing the whole lifecycle.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Distinguishes interim constitutions from genuinely lifecycle-aware design — the gap the proposal targets.

insights.claim: The global population of constitutions already constitutes de facto governance at global scale through repeated language and copied clauses, and holometabolous modularity would increase cross-borrowing — with constitutional offspring pooling genetic material from all constitutions rather than just two parents — moderating geopolitical differences.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: A speculative but non-obvious channel through which institutional convergence, not treaty-making, produces global governance.
insights.locator: The family resemblances of constitutions today

insights.claim: Committees that draft constitutions already informally copy what has worked historically, such as checks and balances, and compensate for observed failings such as life tenure for judges, so constitutions constitute an evolving population that could be optimized separately for each developmental stage.
insights.speaker: Jonathon Keats
insights.so_what: Constitutional design is already an evolutionary process; making it explicitly modular would raise its rate of improvement.
